tldr: Page 75 presents survey responses from Oregon businesses, organizations, and individuals identifying key barriers to prosperity. Dominant concerns: excessive taxes (especially Climate Protection Plan at $129-132/ton—nation's highest); labor shortages and inadequate workforce development systems; unaffordable childcare crisis; permitting delays and regulatory burden; and competitive disadvantages versus neighboring states. Respondents advocate for corporate tax reform, CPP elimination or significant modification, affordable childcare infrastructure investment, streamlined regulations, and a more business-friendly policy environment.

bullets.text: Steve Deacon documents Oregon's 47th ranking for business-friendliness and Portland's 49th ranking for corporate taxation, attributing the rankings to decades of anti-business attitudes.
Tony Moran provides carbon pricing comparison: Oregon CPP $129/ton versus Quebec $31.91, Connecticut/Washington $60.43, California/Delaware/etc. $20.05, and British Columbia $80.
Ted Lehmann reports Oregon CPP at $132/Carbon Ton is the most expensive carbon tax globally; Canada cancelled their $80/ton program as unaffordable.
Patrick Benavides (Tube Forgings) warns CPP failure would force 20-25% production workforce reduction via offshore sub-contracting of hot-formed manufacturing.
Kristen Helton documents child care crisis: professionals underpaid/overworked, programs losing enrollment, families unable to afford care despite ERDC subsidies, system unsustainable.
Kylie Nichols identifies theft and property crime as critical barriers to rural business viability; inadequate system accountability creates repeat-offender cycles.
Staci Calkins highlights Oregon's low journeyman-to-apprentice ratio constraining workforce system, while neighboring Idaho and Washington maintain higher ratios.
Jason Brandt (Oregon Restaurant & Lodging Association) notes $1 million CAT exemption from 2019 no longer reflects inflation, increasing tax burden on hospitality sector.
